subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS-REPORTED SPEECH BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING DORION INQUIRY
MR. WOOLLIAMS-REPORTED SPEECH BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING DORION INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the rights of parliament and therefore the rights of every member of parliament. Parliament is the highest court of the land; parliament is a court. Every member of parliament within this jurisdiction is a judge of this court.
My question of privilege arises out of a statement made by the Minister of Justice while addressing the S.G.W.U. students. The statement was reported in the Montreal Gazette dated February 23, and the comment of the minister is in quotation marks. He was referring to the Dorion commission requested by parliament, requested by the members of parliament and therefore requested by this court and the judges of this court. After much argument the government agreed to set up the Dorion commission by order in council P.C. 1964-1819 and amended order in council P.C. 1964-1820. The words of the minister that I say brought parliament into ridicule and contempt and which are prejudicial to the Dorion commission and prejudge the facts and the evidence are as follows;
When all is said and done most of the insinuations made against the government will be proven to be unfounded.
Further he went on to say, in his own case:
My conscience was clear when the inquiry began and it will remain clear when it ends.
I submit that these words amount to contempt because they create an undue interference with the administration of justice in Canada, which department the minister heads. Any undue interference in reference to the evidence, in reference to the witnesses themselves, and particularly any undue interference with reference to the officers of a tribunal which may exercise undue influence amounts to contempt.
I wish to quote from volume 8, third edition, of Halsbury's Laws of England. Paragraph 16 bears the heading "Obstructing officers of the court" and is as follows:
Contempt by obstructing an officer of the court is punished, not for the purpose of vindicating the dignity of the court or the person of the officer, but to prevent undue interference with the administration of justice.
I ask the question, Mr. Speaker. Did the minister exercise, by words now published in the Gazette, undue interference with the administration of justice as far as the Dorion inquiry is concerned? I now refer to the terms and conditions of the amended order in council dated November 27, 1964, P.C. 1964-1820, and I quote in part:
To inquire fully into allegations about any improper inducements having been offered to or improper pressures having been brought to bear on counsel acting upon an application for the extradition of one Lucien Rivard and all the relevant circumstances connected therewith-
And this is important.
-including the manner in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and any officer thereof and the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice dealt with the allegations when they were brought to their attention.
I now wish to refer to a decision of Mr. Justice Owens of the Quebec Queen's bench division, the case of Sommer v. The Queen, 40 Criminal Reports, page 426:
To speak generally, contempt of court may be said to be constituted by any conduct that tends to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect or disregard, or to interfere with or prejudice parties litigant of their witnesses during the litigation.
Oswald, at page 5, cites from the case of Miller v. Knox (1838) 4 Bing (N.C.) 574, also found in 132 English reports, 910, the following:
"It is defined or described to be a disobedience to the court, an opposing or a despising the authority, justice, or dignity thereof. It commonly consists in a party's doing otherwise than he is enjoined to do, or not doing what he is commanded or required by the process, order, or decree of the court."
There is the often cited statement of Lord Hardwicke, Lord Chancellor, in the St. James' Evening Post case (1742), 2 Atk. 471, also reported in English reports, 683:
"There are three different sorts of contempt. One kind of contempt is scandalizing the court itself. There may be likewise a contempt of this court, in abusing parties who are concerned in

Question of Privilege
causes here. There may be also a contempt of this court, in prejudicing mankind against persons before the cause is heard."
That is important because these statements of which I complain were made by the minister at this meeting before the matter was heard and before a judgment was rendered.
Again at page 91 Oswald states the matter as follows:
"Ail publications which offend against the dignity of the court, or are calculated to prejudice the course of justice, will constitute contempts. Offences of this nature are of three kinds-namely, those which scandalize the court; or abuse the parties concerned in causes there; or prejudice mankind against persons before the cause is heard. Under the first head fall libels on the integrity of the court, its judges, officers, or proceedings; under the second and third heads anything which tends to excite prejudice against the parties, or their litigation, while it is pending."
Other descriptions and definitions of contempt of court are set out in the notes of my colleague Mr. Justice Rivard which I will not repeat.
Then reference is made to several authorities, including McLeod v. Aubyn, (1899) appeal cases, 549. The justice of the court then refers to many authorities.
From these authorities it would appear that a criminal contempt of court has two basic aspects, one consisting of acts or publications which bring the court or judge into contempt, and the other of acts or publications which interfere with or obstruct the course of justice.
The terms of reference in the inquiry approved by parliament directed Mr. Justice Dorion to inquire fully into not only the alleged bribery case but into the manner in which the officials of the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice dealt with those allegations and other allegations in question. I want to repeat that; that under the terms of reference the commissioner was directed to inquire into the manner in which the officials of the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice dealt with those allegations, and these matters are under review before that inquiry now. This statement was made before the evidence was complete, before the minister gave evidence-if he is going to give evidence-and before the judgment was made.
As I see it in brief, the administration of justice in this regard, the Minister of Justice in this regard, and therefore the government, were being tried on an issue to determine whether they had accepted their responsibility and were administering the law of the land impartially and without prejudice. Therefore when the minister made his remarks he unduly interfered with the administration of justice, or at least endeavoured to interfere unduly with the administration of
[Mr. Woolliams.j
justice because he, the minister, caused to be published by his words an article in the newspaper which could unduly interfere with the administration of justice.
He used words in his speech which (1) attempted to prejudge and prejudice the decision, and attempted to prejudge the judicial inquiry; (2) prejudiced himself as a witness, for his opinions now reported in the newspaper which show that the minister might have preconceived political ideas and motives and, even giving him the best benefit of the doubt, may tend to colour, shape and trim his evidence on the facts of which he has personal knowledge. In his position as minister he has exercised influence over public opinion so that the public have now prejudged themselves the evidence of the inquiry prior to judgment being rendered by that said inquiry.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, he has talked; he has intervened when he should have remained silent and aloof as Minister of Justice in this matter. Justice must not only be done but it must seem and appear to be done, and I say by his words in his speech before those students he prejudiced and interfered with the administration of justice so far as that inquiry is concerned.
We shall be interested in the next 24 hours in the attitude of the Prime Minister in this regard. If by his silence or by his words he approves the minister's conduct, then he himself is placed in a similar position, and one must deduce that the code of ethics laid down by the Prime Minister for his ministers is mere words, and that his edicts and memos as to political morality are meaningless.
Will the Prime Minister act now in reference to the statements made on that occasion before that student body, interfering with the administration of justice, and attempting to prejudice the tribunal, the Dorion commission?

It is true that I have not discussed any fact, any allegation brought before the Dorion commission. Naturally, in the course of my remarks I did say with regard to the insinuations-and we have heard quite a few here- to the innuendoes being spread all around,

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF PROPOSAL FOR SECOND HEAVY WATER PLANT

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF PROPOSAL FOR SECOND HEAVY WATER PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the undertaking I gave the house last week I would like to make a statement regarding heavy water production in Canada.
Hon. members will recall that in December, 1963 I advised the house of the government's acceptance of the proposal submitted by Deuterium of Canada Limited to construct and operate a plant to produce heavy water in Canada. The government undertook to underwrite the sale by Deuterium of Canada Limited of 1,000 tons of heavy water, to be produced at a rate of not less than 200 tons per year. Construction of this plant is proceeding on schedule.
Since that decision was taken it has become apparent that the production capacity of the Deuterium of Canada Limited plant would be quite insufficient to meet the domestic demand for heavy water by itself. Accordingly the government decided to encourage the construction of further plant facilities by inviting further proposals.
The government has decided to accept a proposal submitted by Western Deuterium Company Limited, which offers a sale price for heavy water at $14.65 per pound. This is significantly lower than the prices submitted by other bidders. Western Deuterium Company Limited, a wholly Canadian owned British Columbia company, will locate the new plant at Estevan, Saskatchewan.
The plant is to have a capacity to produce 300 tons of heavy water per annum, and the government of Canada will underwrite the sale of the first five years of production at this rate. The company will utilize the maximum possible quantities of Canada materials and equipment, will employ a Canadian owned and directed engineering firm in the construction of the plant, and will employ Canadian citizens in the operation of the plant.
The significantly lower sale price of heavy water to which I have referred is made possible by reason of the intention of Western Deuterium Company Limited to employ a new production process rather than the here-

tofore conventional hydrogen sulphide process. The government has instructed Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to satisfy itself that the employment of this process will guarantee an output of heavy water sufficient to meet the requirements of the invitation, and the acceptance of Western Deuterium Company Limited's proposal is necessarily subject to A.E.C.L.'s endorsement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. In view of the fact that the national capital commission has just expropriated property overlooking the Lebreton flats area on which the new Department of National Defence headquarters building will be constructed, will the minis-

ter inform the house why the national capital commission withheld expropriation until the construction of an apartment building on that site had been started, and after expensive architectural plans had been completed and $350,000 spent in purchasing the property, all of which will necessitate an unnecessary reimbursement from taxpayers' money?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: EXPROPRIATION OF LAND ON WHICH APARTMENT CONSTRUCTION HAD BEGUN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as plans for the reconstruction of Lebreton flats became known it became evident to the national capital commission that the property recently expropriated should form part of the Lebreton complex. As my hon. friend has stated, the headquarters of the national defence department will be located there, forming only a portion of the complete government complex to be located in this area. In view of the fact that a considerable amount of money had to be expended in that area it was felt that it would be wiser on the part of the government to expropriate the piece of land to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I might state that the new zoning bylaw would permit the construction of a building some 150 feet high on this promontory. Had that occurred the whole architectural plan involving the rest of Lebreton flats would have been compromised. For that reason it was felt to be in the public interest to expropriate this property at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the growing concern in Canada over the early expiry of the period in which persons can be charged with war offences in West Germany, would the minister tell the house the policy of the government in the matter, and whether the policy of the government has been communicated to the Bonn government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: WEST GERMANY-TIME LIMITATION ON TRIALS FOR WAR CRIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision in this matter, of course, is one that rests with the federal republic of West Germany. However, the Canadian government has been advised by the Bonn government that under present German law these trials will not cease after May, 1965. Persons guilty of war crimes may be prosecuted for years after that date if their names are before the courts by May 8 of this year.
The German authorities have assured us they are satisfied that legal action has already been taken or begun against the vast majority of German war criminals. However, I should

Inquiries of the Ministry say to my hon. friend that the government shares his concern and that of others with regard to the effect of the statute of limitations, and conversations between Canada and other wartime allies and the German government are under way.

subtopic: ALBERTA-INQUIRY AS TO PROTEST MARCH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Would the minister advise the house on the proposed protest march of the Indians in northern Alberta? This is of immediate concern and is related as well to the Cree band at Fort Chipewyan, who are faced with a severe economic problem due to the increase in population and the decrease in their sources of self employed income, and who are requesting reserve facilities at present denied to them.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: ALBERTA-INQUIRY AS TO PROTEST MARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of his question. It is not a proposed march; it was an actual trek that took place yesterday. Some 110 or 111 Indians are in
Inquiries of the Ministry Edmonton today and will probably be there tomorrow.
In order to deal with the matter effectively I might refer briefly to this particular band of Indians. Hay Lakes is located in the northwestern part of Alberta. It is readily accessible only by air and is a typical isolated bush community whose eventual development will depend on the provision of road access to resources and markets. At the moment some 40-odd members of the band are provided with jobs cutting pulpwood but 85 per cent of the band are still suffering economic difficulties because of the nature of soil, topography and other conditions that exist.
I should like to assure the hon. member and other members interested that the report in last night's paper that there is real hardship with a threat of starvation is extreme and untrue. I should also like to assure the house that the 110 or so Indians involved are behaving in a very orderly manner and are discussing their claims with the government of Alberta and with senior representatives of my department with dignity and great restraint. Discussions with regional officers of the department are and will be continuing today and tomorrow. We have asked the chief of our economic development branch to proceed west tonight, and he will be participating tomorrow in the discussions with the Alberta government, the Indians themselves and the regional officers of the department.
With regard to the other reserve referred to by my hon. friend, that at Fort Chipewyan, Alberta, I might say that the Cree band who occupy that reserve has a land entitlement under treaty No. 8 which has never been met. The circumstances there are rather special. I might also say that the chief of the band, Chief Cowie, wrote my predecessor and made a request or inquired as to the possibilities of securing some land in the Wood Buffalo national park. Negotiations are going on between the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Alberta government regarding this park, and I have asked for a report on them. If I have anything further of interest to report I will make a statement at a later date.

subtopic: ALBERTA-INQUIRY AS TO PROTEST MARCH
speechtext:
supplementary question. I should like to ask the minister whether it is true that the band at Hay Lakes had on previous occasions asked the department to help develop an economic program, and that the only response it received from the department was an offer of more welfare which they really did not want.

Inquiries of the Ministry Second, I should like to ask whether the premier of Alberta has wired the government asking for assistance and, if so, what response the government has made.

subtopic: ALBERTA-INQUIRY AS TO PROTEST MARCH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hasten to deny the suggestion that the department has done nothing. The department has been in close contact with the Indians themselves as well as with the government of Alberta. Discussions have advanced to the stage that they have set up an Indian friendship centre in Calgary for the province of Alberta, and these economic questions have been or are being referred to this friendship centre for study. The Indians are represented as well as both senior levels of government.

subtopic: ALBERTA-INQUIRY AS TO PROTEST MARCH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister whether it is correct, as reported in the press, that the premier of Alberta has wired the Prime Minister asking for action; and if that is correct does it not raise some question with regard to the minister's assurance that the province of Alberta is apparently satisfied with the action his department is taking?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answering that question, with the approval of the Prime Minister, I believe I can say that a wire was received. Mr. Chairman, it is my view that the position occupied by commercial fishermen should be considered under the terms of subsequent clauses. However, in view of the fact that this subject has now been discussed during our consideration of clause 2, in respect of which an amendment has been proposed, I should like to make a few observations.
The cause of the fishermen on the west coast and, as has been indicated, the fishermen in other areas, is one which deserves the full consideration of this house, particularly as it relates to the terms of this Canada pension plan. It was the intention of this plan to bring as many Canadian workers as possible under its provisions, and when one considers fishermen and their peculiar problems he must come to the conclusion that they also deserve consideration.
This matter was dealt with in some detail in the brief presented to the special committee by the united fishermen and allied workers

union, which is an organization representing and speaking for a large part of the fishing industry on the west coast. May I say that this union has done a commendable job in representing the fishermen of that area.
At page 13 of their brief they have called the special committee's attention to some recommended amendments to Bill C-136 which they feel necessary if this plan is to meet the requirements of fishermen and make them eligible for benefits.
Very briefly their recommended amendments are as follows:
(1)	Inclusion of all commercial fishermen in the definition of employment considered to be pensionable employment, notwithstanding that some fishermen may not appear legally to be employees.
(2)	Inclusion as employers of fishermen any fishing company, co-operative or person with whom fishermen enter into contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of their occupations as fishermen.
(3)	All such other matters as are necessary to provide that commercial fishermen are included in the Canada pension plan, with the normal employers share of the contribution being paid by the fish processing companies and co-operatives.
Following these recommendations the brief outlines the reasons why these amendments are not only necessary but desirable and warranted.
This matter has been discussed by a number of members in the house both on the opposition and government sides, and at least the principle has been supported by those hon. members. I should like at this time to indicate my support of the principle that has been enunciated, to the effect that commercial fishermen should have status under the Canada pension plan similar to or the same as that which they occupy under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I recognize the fact that all factors are not parallel, but I believe they are parallel at least to the extent that this suggestion should be taken into consideration. It does seem rather strange that there should be different interpretations in two federal statutes.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard stated that he felt the representations made on behalf of the fishermen should be studied thoroughly with a view to bringing the fishermen within the terms of the Canada pension plan before the governor in council drafts the regulations. As pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena, perhaps that should have been sufficient to meet the situation, but I feel the fishermen would be taking a rather large chance in leaving their requests in that uncertain position. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I feel the amendment which has

been introduced is worthy of the consideration and support of this committee.

The amount of the earnings to be used for this purpose would be the income from his occupation or endeavour as such income is computed under the Income Tax Act. Essentially it is the net income after deducting from his gross income the amounts of his operating expenses and his capital cost allowance. Computations on selfemployed earnings are determined on the basis of an annual return filed by the contributor along with his income tax return.
The only specific reference to fishing in this particular bill is the exclusion from pensionable employment under the provisions of paragraph (a) of subclause 2 of clause 6 for limited amounts of earnings, that is, less than $250 in cash remuneration or working for a period of less than 25 working days. It will therefore be apparent that subject to this limitation all commercial fishermen are covered by the Canada pension plan either as being in pensionable employment or as being in receipt of self-employed earnings.
In addition, clause 7 gives the governor in council the power to make regulations for including persons in pensionable employment or excluding persons therefrom, but these powers are restricted to the specific wording contained in the various paragraphs included thereunder. Specifically, paragraph (d) of subclause 1 and paragraph (e) of subclause 2 give the governor in council the power to make a regulation determining whether or not the terms on which services are performed are analogous to a contract of service or to the earning of income from his business as the case may be. The wording of paragraph (d) of subclause 1 is as follows:
(d) the performance of services for remuneration if it appears to the governor in council that the terms or conditions on which the services are performed and the remuneration is paid are analogous to a contract of service, whether or not they constitute a contract of service.
A regulation under any of these clauses would only be made after an adequate study of the circumstances. The amendment proposed by the hon. member would provide that an employee shall include any person who is engaged in fishing, whether or not he is actually an employee or whether or not the form of the contract is such as could be reasonably regarded as analogous to a contract of service. I presume that the mover of the amendment is aware that all commercial fishermen are covered under the Canada pension plan as it is now worded and therefore the only purpose of the amendment could be

Canada Pension Plan
to shift part of the contribution from a selfemployed person to the buyer of his product.
I am not in favour of this amendment for the following reasons, and I will give several reasons for not being in favour of it. First of all, this amendment would create many problems of administration, the first of which is that effectively it could not be enforced. Marketing methods of commercial fishermen are not necessarily the same across Canada and many instances would arise where the purchasers or processors are not in Canada. In other instances, fish is packed and shipped to a buyer distant from the fishermen and the buyer would have no way of knowing who were the persons who were entitled to share in the proceeds. Also, problems would arise as to who would make an employer's contribution in an instance where one fisherman sells fish to another fisherman for bait purposes.
Second, other difficulties would arise as to the amount of earnings upon which the contributions should be made. The income of a fisherman cannot be determined correctly from the amount received from the sale of his fish, since expenses have to be taken into consideration as well as capital cost allowance and so on. Again, since the methods of fishing differ in various parts of Canada there is no set percentage that could be allowed for expenses that would be suitable.
Third, because of the variety of arrangements in the fishing industry and the number of different people to whom a catch may be sold, there would be extreme difficulties in maintaining the record of earnings for each fisherman provided under the Canada pension plan.
Contributions and earnings would have to be accumulated in the first instance on the basis of information supplied by the purchasers as to the contributions and earnings of each fisherman. At the present time there is no procedure under the Income Tax Act for collecting contributions from purchasers of fish or for obtaining from such persons an annual statement of contributions and earnings of each fisherman from whom the fish purchases might be made.
Also, because of the variety of circumstances under which fish is sold the accuracy of the information received from the suppliers would be in great doubt. Benefits under the Canada pension plan in the normal case are determined from the earnings and contributions as recorded in the record of earnings over the lifetime of the contributor, and we could not rely on the fisherman mak-

ing inquiries as to the amount credited to him in the record of earnings periodically as is provided in the plan. There is an essential difference in this respect between the determination of benefits under this plan and under the Unemployment Insurance Act in respect of which benefits accrue after a comparatively short period and are only calculated where there is a claim because of unemployment.
Fourth, because of the many methods that are in operation regarding the sharing of a catch it is difficult for the fish buyer to ascertain the proportions that should be allocated to each person who is sharing in the catch. There would be insurmountable difficulties in determining what proportion of the basic exemption should be allowed, since a fish purchaser would have no way of knowing over what period the fish purchase was caught, and it would be impossible to determine when the maximum contribution had been reached for a year unless the fishing companies maintained a specific record for this purpose.
It is also understood that in some instances fishermen sell their products to different buyers in the course of a year because of the different kinds of fish that are landed and, in some cases, to several buyers in the course of a week. This would multiply the problems that relate to refunds of contributions.
If this amendment were passed there would be discrimination between fishermen and those in other lines of endeavour. As I have already mentioned, a farmer who is raising hogs or cattle might claim that he should be regarded as an employee and the packing company as his employer. Similar requests might be made from grain farmers who sell to the wheat pool or persons in service industries such as independent taxi drivers, proprietors of gasoline service stations and others. They could all maintain that the person to whom they sell their product or who supplies their product should really be considered as their employer.
There would also be discrimination in the manner in which the earnings of fishermen are calculated, compared with other selfemployed persons. As previously mentioned, if this amendment were passed the earnings of a fisherman would have to be determined arbitrarily as a percentage of his gross receipts. There would, therefore, be a departure from the basic principle that the Canada pension plan is an earnings related plan. For

1163T
all of the above reasons, Mr. Chairman, I am not in favour of this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to continue the discussion on clause 2. I am impressed with the seriousness with which the committee is considering this very significant bill, because I am aware that when it becomes law very serious measures will have been launched which, in all practicability, will be irreversible. For this reason I feel the joint committee which examined the bill should be lauded for the very judicious work it undertook during the recess.
Certainly the fact that they devoted the initial series of their meetings to studying the complex clauses of the bill points out that it is a measure of utmost complexity and few of us-I am one-really completely understand it fully. In fact I believe it is too complex for all hon. members to understand the complexities of all clauses in the bill. For this reason I say we must proceed with caution because our undertaking is a very serious one. It certainly affects all Canadians, even those who are not themselves beneficiaries under the plan.
Having said that, I must point out that the short title, the "Canada pension plan", is rather misleading because the full title refers to "old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors." We must underline the fact that the plan is not for all Canadians but for contributors only. This is sometimes where the error in public understanding creeps in, because we were expecting a measure, according to the white paper issued by the minister in August, to establish a contributory pension plan insuring that as soon as possible and in a fair and practical way all Canadians would be able to look forward to retiring in security with dignity.
It is now quite apparent that not all Canadians are included in this measure. Those significant groups which are omitted were named by hon. members yesterday, and it has been pointed out to the committee that this is a problem which cannot very well be fitted into the proposed measure. However, I am confident the committee will consider a definite series of amendments proposed to improve the bill as presently drafted.
The general endorsement of the plan that our party gave it on second reading, and which I still feel inclined to give it, spoke of coverages that are really quite generous. These are going to be possible only because of the vast cumulative amounts of money that will have to be collected from contributors, and because of this vast amount of money involved-we have heard estimates of $6 billion being in the fund at the end of 10 years-I repeat my plea for a consideration of priorities, priorities in the general field of public welfare and health and education.
I am speaking of these things by way of general comment, but I feel justified in making reference to priorities because the federal system under which we operate permits taxation in the same areas in both the federal and provincial fields. I give the example of income tax. Both the provincial and federal governments can impose a tax on personal income, and the same is true with respect to corporation income. Then there are other tax areas in which there are separate divisions, for example provincial sales taxes, and customs and excise taxes, the first being restricted to the realms of the provinces and the latter to that of the federal government. It has been pointed out by persons more knowledgeable than myself that these combined sources of taxation now take in something like 35 per cent of the

Canada Pension Plan
gross national product. There is a vast sum of money involved, and common sense demands from us that we get the best value for our dollars spent. I should like to emphasize that we need to be cautious. Perhaps I may quote from the brief which was presented to the committee by the Canadian welfare council. I read from page 3 of the submission:
No intelligent assessment of a proposed social security program can be made unless the assessment takes into account the rapidly changing social order. At the risk of stating the obvious, it is noted that Canada like most other nations in the world today is having to examine values and concepts which, while serving admirably in the past, no longer hold as central a position as they once did. Indeed, the whole development of social security as we now know it and accept it is. from this point of view, a continual adaptation to changing social values and situations.
The long term implications of the Canada pension plan and the basic role envisaged for it in Canada's pattern of social security make it essential to assess the plan in the light of probable future social and economic circumstances.
The welfare council makes some valid comments on the social implications of the plan and these, too, are worthy of consideration. When I think of expenditures I think at once of expenditures in the field of education, because this is where the greatest returns will eventually be found. However, if I were to continue on this subject I am afraid I would be straying beyond the confines of clause 2. I merely wish to point out that we may sometimes be placing too much emphasis on the needs of the wrong segment of the population. What we are really doing by this measure is taxing young Canadians so as to provide benefits for older citizens.
Considerable benefits will certainly accrue as a result of this scheme. At the same time there are significant difficulties and some of these difficulties have already been brought to the attention of the committee. One feature which appeals to me greatly is the contributory nature of this plan. Too often today we hear people saying that the government should do this, or the government should do that-a continual attitude of "gimme, gimme". The benefits foreseen under the Canadian pension plan are not in the nature of a straight handout from the government to senior citizens, but something they are receiving in return for contributions made. But this is where the fairness ends. There are many discrepancies which are bound to arise under the system now contemplated. What I am trying to say is that the relation of the contribution to the ultimate benefits is not, in many cases, really fair. I would just draw
EMr. Enns.]
attention to the windfalls which accrue to older people. To give an obvious example, a person who has contributed for ten years at the maximum rate, which is almost $80 a year, has paid in almost $800 in that period. Yet the first year in which he is eligible for pension he will get, possibly, ten times $104, or $1,040. In other words, in the first year he more than recovers the contribution he has made during the ten year period. This is an unfair windfall and for this reason I say the contributions are not fairly related to the benefits expected.

I would suggest that at the end of 47 years, when all today's 18 year olds are in receipt of pensions, there may be some form of equity. Even then I fear this will not be the case, because there are so many exemptions and qualifications attached to the period of contributions, taking into account the best ten years of earnings and the like. I am wondering how members of parliament will deal with constituents who write to them and say: My neighbour, who is just as old as I am, is receiving $2.37 more than I receive, though I believe I am in the same circumstances. I feel our task in assisting constituents with regard to questions of this kind will be greatly increased. Again I acknowledge there will have to be inequities, because at no time can any measure such as this be completely equitable. Nevertheless I am drawing attention to some of the difficulties. I certainly still endorse the plan, but 47 years seems a long time to wait for the full fruition of this scheme.
Another area of concern is the manner in which the plan will be integrated with private plans-I am putting this in reverse because, of course, private plans will have to be integrated with the Canada pension plan, I suppose. As a result, I think there will be a shifting of private plans and a difficult adjustment period before everyone is happy with the situation.
Hon. members who have already spoken have asked for an economic report to show just how this scheme will affect the economy of the country. I am interested to know whether or not we shall be given such a report. It would also be extremely interest-

ing to know the attitude of the royal commission on taxation with regard to this plan. I feel we are on the doorstep of vast changes in our taxation structure and it is a valid expectation that we should be made aware of the attitude which such an important commission takes toward the federal plan. I would also remind the committee that the royal commission on banking and finance has commented on the Canada pension plan, pointing out that even though the per capita income of Canadians is something like 30 per cent below the per capita income of the United States, the Canadian plan undertakes none the less to provide benefits considerably in excess of those available under the United States social security scheme. This comparison worries me. I wish to emphasize that, though we talk about a 3.6 per cent contribution and an over-all pension benefit of $179, we should keep in mind the contribution made by the existing 4 per cent social security tax. So already we are paying 7.6 per cent for this pension of $179, which is not very different from the cost of the United States scheme. However, we hear rumours and reports on good authority that United States costs are rising and will likely increase to almost 9 per cent in the present year. I think therefore there is cause to worry, inasmuch as the scale of contribution may have to be increased in the future-

I am sure the minister agrees that it is in the interests of all Canadians and all members of this house that we proceed very carefully, clause by clause, with this very important legislation. Before I deal with the main topic of my remarks this afternoon I would like to mention something touched upon by the previous speaker, namely the necessity for governments to plan priorities. I cannot escape making a comment on this matter at the present time. I think most of us in public life now realize that the electorate feel that governments do not hand out anything any more. Moreover they recognize that governments merely collect and administer tax dollars; and today most people recognize that if we are going to alleviate some of the problems and conditions facing the country, governments, be it the federal government or provincial governments, are going to have to spend vast and vaster sums of money. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, when we are talking about medicare, when we are talking about education, when we are talking about the expenditures involved in a plan such as we are analysing today, I think more and more we must underline the necessity and importance of the federal government and the provinces meeting as soon as possible to plan their priorities.
I only wish to add my support to this idea. It is certainly not the first time it has been mentioned; Premier Roblin of Manitoba has mentioned it time and time again. I think everybody should recognize that big government is not necessarily a bad thing and should welcome large government expenditures in a country like Canada, where consumer spending is at an all-time high. Because of this situation we must time and time again underline the necessity for the planning of priorities in the field of public expenditures, be they federal, provincial or joint expenditures.
I believe it has already been pointed out that many people on this side of the house are concerned with one general proposition, namely that a vast number of Canadians living in grinding poverty and want are not going to be covered by this scheme. I would like to assure the minister in all sincerity that I am not going to discuss this matter in a partisan sense at all; but I believe this is a time when we should underline this whole situation. I say this because, generally speaking, when we discuss social legislation

in the broadest sense of that word, I do not believe I am exaggerating when I say that we usually think this social legislation, whether it is in connection with health or welfare, is going to benefit many citizens in our society who are among the less fortunate. I think that as we go on in our thinking we should pinpoint some of the facts in relation to this problem as it relates to a pension plan.
I believe it is a bad thing when people in responsible positions, such as the Minister of Finance, say we have never had it so good. I think it is a bad thing to say that in a country like Canada, where far too many people are living in grinding poverty and want. I ask myself many, many-

Mr. Chairman, I am going to touch upon this subject in a minute. The hon. member has raised a very, very good point, which I fully understand. However, I feel very strongly about this question. Very often we quote statistics in the House of Commons with regard to what the gross national product is going to be, and so on, when we discuss social legislation-and all of us are guilty of this. But for my part I should say that many people who visit my office in the country, because I am their member of parliament, have never fallen under the aegis of government or private welfare help. Many people who come into my office would not know where the unemployment insurance office is; they have not seen a book or an unemployment insurance stamp. I say that we should not fool ourselves in this respect.
The hon. member who just asked me this question referred, in a speech he made in the house a few days ago, to the late President Kennedy, who spoke of the voiceless, silent poor who very rarely were covered by government or private schemes. My only reason for taking up the time of the committee this afternoon is to again issue the warning that has been issued many times in the last few weeks by the Minister of Forestry, namely that we should not fool ourselves that by passing certain social legislation we are in any way coming to grips with the problem of poverty that is facing this country today.
Going back to my original remarks, Mr Chairman, I ask this question: Am I not right in saying that classically speaking and tra-

ditionally speaking, when we pass social legislation do we not usually-I am referring to social legislation in the true sense of that word-think we are passing legislation to help those people who need help the most?
All I can say is that I hope when we have voted on this bill and the vast expenditures of money which will be voted have been made, there will still be some public funds left over to really do battle with the question of poverty in Canada.
I am going to pinpoint this question of poverty in Canada and then ask the minister and the government to give us a general idea of how many people in this general area she thinks will be covered by the proposed plan.
I intend to go further and say this. Mass poverty is one thing in African and Asian countries, but it is yet another thing in Canada where we have at the present time the second highest economic standard of living in the world.
It is my impression, Mr. Chairman, that millions of Canadians are not truly sharing in our nation's prosperity. I think this has been the situation under all governments up to the present time. Right here at home we have done a poor job in pushing back the frontiers of poverty and want. Many people talk about the concept of individual and national excellence. This concept will be or is meaningless to the millions of Canadians who barely exist, or should I say subsist, under substandard conditions.
I hope, sir, that while we are discussing this bill in the broadest sense of the word we will realize that it is not coming to grips with the basic question of poverty in Canada, which is something most social legislation should and can do. I hope that we shall realize that we must put an end to poverty in the midst of plenty. Otherwise, sir, what will our answer be to communism abroad?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre quoted some statistics in this regard yesterday. I followed up those statistics with some brief remarks, enlarging upon them. under $3,000, and that deprivation means families of four persons with total annual incomes under $4,000. I ask the minister to give us some idea, as we proceed with our consideration, as to her view of what portion of that 35 per cent group is going to be covered by this proposed legislation.

They are the silent, voiceless poor who have never known economic opportunity. As I said in my answer, they rarely, if ever, have been in unemployment insurance offices. They do not know what an unemployment insurance book looks like. What does a prosperous Canada mean to these people? What does the Minister of Finance's remark that we have never had it so good mean to them? I should simply like to say this. When conditions such as these exist in a country which enjoys the second highest economic standard of living in the world, we as members of parliament ought to be pretty careful when we quote statistics.
The gross national product may be up and unemployment may be down, yet these people I am referring to still remain poor. I do not wish to be irresponsible in any references I make, but I want to be satisfied by the minister that this is not a piece of legislation which is going to make the semi-affluent more affluent and the rich richer, and completely forget the poor of this nation.

Mr. Chairman, I am prompted to rise this afternoon for two reasons. First of all, last evening the hon. member for Middlesex West quoted a statement from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of February 18 with which I am afraid I cannot agree 20220-737i
Canada Pension Plan
-not with the first part of it anyway. That statement was:
The special Senate committee which studied the proposed Canada pension plan during the recess has not been very lavish with its recommendations for improvements.
The implication is that no recommendations were made and this, of course, I deny categorically. When I was speaking yesterday afternoon my time was somewhat confined because of the disturbance, I suppose we might call it, which arose, and I was not able to state the recommendations that my party had made during the committee meetings. I should like to state those now.
First of all, my party supports the suggestion that a flat rate benefit of $25 monthly should be taken from the Canada pension plan funds to assist all persons over the age of 70 who are receiving old age security benefits. This of course is intended to assist those who are now retired. I also support the proposition that persons from 65 to 70 who have retired from regular employment shall receive an additional uniform flat rate amount of up to $25 a month to be paid from the Canada pension plan funds. These recommendations were made.
These two groups contain people whom the Canada pension plan completely forgets, save for the small cost of living bonus. In my view they deserve at least as good treatment as Canadians who retire under the Canada pension plan. They are a large part of that one and a quarter million I mentioned who 10 years after the plan begins will be getting nothing from the plan. The rest of that one and a quarter million will be people who never earned, or earned so little that they never paid. To help these people my party proposes, and so recommended in the committee, that no one, regardless of income, shall be excluded from the Canada pension plan, and those persons earning less than the eligibility minimum of $600 for employees and $800 for self-employed should be credited with their actual earnings for the purpose of determining the pension which they will be entitled to draw without making a contribution.
To ensure that pensions will never be at the exceedingly low level of $2.50 monthly, which will be drawn by those earning as low as $100 a month in 1967, and to minimize the effect of extending the transitional period to 20 years, my party suggests that all persons qualifying for any pension benefit under the act shall receive, subject to an appropriate residence test, a minimum pension of $25 a

Canada Pension Plan
month in the case of a single person and $40 a month in the case of a married couple. We suggest that this $40 a month for couples continue until the wife reaches the age when she will draw her old age security allowance. If I remember correctly, the best figures the department could provide indicated that wives are on average 4.2 years younger than their husbands. This means that this couple would for as long as four years have to live on a rather low income rate, if something is not done to correct this situation. It is for this reason that we suggest it should be $40 a couple till the wife reaches the point where she draws her old age security benefits.
Finally, it is a definitely wrong principle to discriminate against students. It is very wrong indeed to penalize those who take advanced educational courses when developments in science and industry are so dependent upon the contributions which these young people can make to the nation. We were pleased that the committee saw fit to accept, in part, our recommendation, which was also made by others, that the dropout years should be increased in calculating the earnings base. The committee did suggest that the dropout percentages should be raised from 10 to 20 per cent. However, this does not completely meet the needs of students who may be in university or technical college until as late a year as 25. This time in school will, in effect, use up seven of the nine years of dropout which they are allowed under the new 20 per cent arrangement.
We believe that a student between the ages of 18 and 25 should at his own option not be required to make contributions in each of those years in which he is registered as a full time student at a recognized educational institution, in which case the years in which such person did not make contributions should not be included in determining his lifetime earnings.
I had intended, Mr. Chairman, to say more, but probably with what I said yesterday and what I have said today I have used up about as much of the time of the committee as I am entitled to. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of saying a few words at this time on what I feel may turn out to be one of Canada's most important pieces of social legislation since confederation. Everyone, whether old or young, single or married, will agree that the welfare of our nation's old people, the disabled, and so on, in this and in future generations is a matter of vital concern to us all. I am also certain they will agree that the enactment of a pension plan to assist this age group can be amongst the greatest moves which this or any future parliament can make.
Since the plan was first advanced I have had numerous letters on the subject from people within my riding and from outside my riding, from businessmen and labourers and from people who stand to receive major benefits and those who expect to gain very little. Most of these people seem to be agreed on at least one point-that the plan as outlined by our government and which was worked on by members from all parties in committee for a number of weeks recently has considerable merit. They see it as a step in the right direction, as a move to provide financial security for Canadians in their twilight years. Like the speaker who preceded me, I also hope to support this bill.
However, many of these writers have pointed out that while they feel there are shortcomings in the plan set up by the government, some of these minor faults, if I may call them that, have been corrected by the committee which laboured so hard for so many weeks. But many of the people with whom I have been in contact, as well as members in my own party, believe that further improvements should be made before the bill becomes law. I think it is my duty as the representative of the people in the riding of Waterloo North and as a member of Canada's parliament to bring forward these criticisms and suggestions regarding changes in the bill, with the hope that the best possible plan can be drawn up to benefit the greatest number of people.
Probably the chief criticism is that the scheme gives little or nothing to those who are in the greatest need, and provides the most for those who have the most. Payment is based not on need but rather on income. Those now retired receive nothing. Many of

them, particularly those in the higher age bracket, spent a great part of their earning years during the depression-I hope that will not be forgotten-when it was practically impossible to salt away any savings for later life. Many of these same people were unfortunate to be working in an age when private pension plans were relatively rare. Today many thousands of these people who formed the backbone of our country in the dark days of depression, through the war years and in the adjustment to a peace time economy are struggling to eke out an existence until they can qualify for the old age pension.
May I ask, Mr. Chairman, does a government have a greater responsibility to those who will be retiring in the future than to those now retired? May I repeat that: Does a government have a greater responsibility to those who will be retiring in the future than to those now retired? While today's retired get nothing, the man who finishes his working days after contributing to the plan for only ten years can receive what has been termed by many as a windfall or an unearned bonus. For example, a person at the maximum earnings limits of $5,000 who retires at age 65 after contributing for only ten years will have paid about $1,000 into the plan, but his pension will be worth more than $18,000.
I think it is important too to point out that those whose average earnings are consistently lower than the minimum set out in the bill receive no benefits. These unfortunate Canadians, who form some 5 per cent of the work force, will be unable to provide for their own retirement. It is also my feeling, Mr. Chairman, that while the plan overlooks those now retired and those in greatest need, it also penalizes students, as was mentioned by my comrade who preceded me. According to the plan envisaged by our government, a person's pension is calculated on an average lifetime earnings, but he is allowed to eliminate one tenth of his poorest income years. I understand that the government has accepted one fifth. This penalizes students for the years which they spend as students, during which period they earn only enough in their holidays to finance their education.
How can some of these shortcomings, which I and many others feel are inequities, be overcome? For a few moments let me dwell on some of the recommendations which our party is advancing, and suggestions which I can offer after speaking to some of my constituents and giving considerable thought to the matter.
Canada Pension Plan
First, let us give to those receiving the old age pension of $75 an additional payment of $25. Then we might also give an additional payment of $25 a month to those retired people between 65 and 70 who do not receive the old age pension, as announced by the Prime Minister last Wednesday. I believe that on several occasions I have mentioned the dire need of people between 65 and 70 who, unfortunately, were working for a firm which had no pension plan but who, during their 35 years or so with it, were able to save enough money to buy their homes, but have not enough money left in the bank when they retire. I feel we should give much consideration to these people.
We could also set a minimum pension of $25 a month for single persons, and $40 for married couples. A further suggestion is that persons earning less than the qualifying amount for the plan be credited with their actual earnings so that they can be included in determining the amount of pensions received. This, you may say, would require a bigger outlay if these people were not assessed. However, the plan could be changed so that those whose annual earnings exceed the minimum amounts could contribute on their total earnings.
Costs resulting from these recommendations would of course be higher, but our party feels they could be balanced by a lower implementation of the plan. Lengthening the period for the scheme would also narrow the inequalities between people with high and low earnings, reduce the number of people who would get a pension higher than their previous earnings, make it easier to integrate the plan with private pension schemes, and increase the pension fund available for the provinces to borrow.
Recently a member of the government in an address to a Toronto audience expressed hope that the Canada pension plan would be whipped through parliament as fast as possible and with as few changes as possible. I believe he suggested that failure to speed the bill into law would be a calamity.
As I said previously, Mr. Chairman, this is one of the greatest pieces of legislation we shall be faced with in our time. As I stressed earlier in my remarks, we are now on the threshold of one of the greatest pieces of social legislation in Canada's nearly 100 year history. The plan is of vital importance to every Canadian, regardless of how much or how little he stands to benefit by it. All of us sitting here today have a duty to do all possible to see that the plan is the best one

Canada Pension Plan
possible within our means. The real calamity would not be in failing to push the plan through parliament rapidly, but rather in jamming through the House of Commons a second rate plan, one which we might be ashamed of in years to come.
Built into the bill are safeguards which will make future major changes extremely difficult. Such changes could be effected only with the approval of two thirds of the participating provinces, and then only if they represent two thirds of the people.
So, let us not be hasty, even if it takes days, weeks, months to come up with a top-notch plan. This is just as important as reciprocity, the flag and many other things we have been grumbling about for a long time. I do not care if it takes six months in order that we get a plan whereby all Canadians can benefit, especially those between the ages of 65 and 70 who for long have wanted some social help.
We have before us the framework for legislation which can benefit millions of Canadians for hundreds of years. It is our first and also one of the few national schemes anywhere. Let us make it a plan of which all Canada can be proud, and a working model for other countries throughout the world.

This is to establish a contributory pension plan ensuring that, as soon as is possible in a fair and practical way, all Canadians will be able to look .forward to retiring in security and with dignity.
I still cannot fathom it, but early last week there was an attempt made to indicate to the Canadian people that the government

is in favour of extending the current flat rate old age security payment of $75 a month, on the most peculiar basis of starting the increase at age 69 on January 1 next year and continuing to reduce the age yearly until the entire group between the ages 65 to 70 are covered by that flat rate payment.
We cannot determine here this afternoon the effect this plan will have on the economy of the country. Certainly, we do not expect that Canada, with all its resources and with the future we believe is ahead of us, will in any way lag behind any other of the progressive countries of the world. Therefore there is a need today, and I believe there will be a need in the future, to consider those words which appear in the white paper- "security and dignity". Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for your remarks which created a cooling off period. Several members on the other side of this house have irritated me to the point that I answered with some heat, and strayed from the subject matter before us for consideration. It is unfortunate that those members continue along that line.
As I understand the proposal, Mr. Chairman, contributions are to be made to the Canada pension plan in the amount of 1.8 per cent by both employer and employee. I am sure there are very few members on this side of the house who will not agree with the principle of a Canada pension plan, but let us not deceive ourselves or the public by thinking that contributions in that amount will be sufficient to carry out this pension plan successfully. All one need do to be convinced of that fact is look at the United States social security plans which require payments in the amount of 7.25 per cent, which we understand very shortly will be increased to 9 per cent. Let us not be deceived that the plan with its presently proposed contributions will operate successfully after its institution on January 1, 1966. The Canadian people must be made to understand that fact.
As other hon. members have suggested, there are many things about this plan which must be clarified. I have referred to one such aspect already today and should like again to state it for clarification. I refer of course to the suggestion that $100 per month should be paid to every individual in Canada 65 years of age and over. That suggestion, I believe, is in essence what the Ontario representatives supported and enunciated to the special committee on the Canada pension plan. I believe also that is the idea supported by all members of the Conservative party, particularly those who were members of that committee. In this regard, Mr. Chairman, I will stand on what the record shows.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, it is my belief that many advantageous things can be developed as a result of our consideration of this bill, one of which could be the creation of greater unity in Canada. I suggest once again to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, whom I hold in high regard, that she has the opportunity of making a really big person of herself by showing some leadership in the presentation of a bill which will be accepted by the Canadian public.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is an all party project in spite of the fact that most political parties like to say they were first in thinking of the idea. This is the type of legislative measure which affects every man, woman and child in Canada. All political parties have expressed themselves at one time or another as being in favour of a universal pension plan. On many occasions during the past six years I have publicly advocated such a universal pension plan. However, Mr. Chairman, the plan now before us for consideration is not a universal pension plan.
I represent a rural district comprised largely of farming families, two thirds of which receive incomes of less than $600. In many cases these families do not receive any income at all, and during the past two years particularly have been living at a subsistence level only. This plan will not contribute anything at all to those citizens of Canada. If the plan was universal, as I said, I would support it. I promised to support it and I am one who after an election remembers his election promises and works as hard as he possibly can to bring them into effect.
If this plan offered these people what I have always said I stood for I would be willing to put it through now, but if one third to two thirds of the people in my district cannot benefit under it I cannot go back to them and say that this is the universal plan for which I have fought. At the end of the debate on this subject it may be that because there is a desire to have half a cake rather than no cake at all a good many of us will be in the position that we have to vote for some improvement, and perhaps to certain groups in the country this plan will represent an improvement. I know there are certain people in the 55 to 65 age group who are going to join the Cartwrights on the Bonanza ranch, but because the plan happens to help a few people I do not think we are honour bound to put it through merely because 10 per cent of the population are going to find themselves very well off. The very people I want to help the most are the ones who are going to be helped the least.
Surely those people who have worked all their lives on small bush farms, have reached the age of 60, five years away from the present suggestion, and are no longer able to do hard outdoor work under sub-Arctic weather conditions in the winter should be able to retire and perhaps make way for more efficient farming units. The tendency is in that direction. What are these people going to do?

They certainly cannot move into the thriving cities of Calgary and Edmonton and afford to pay rent, because under reasonable conditions rent would take up the whole of their pension.
I am willing to offer these people half a cake rather than no cake at all, but every member in every party is looking forward to our future today with great faith. We are always boasting about our country having the second highest standard of living in the world. I think we have only scratched our potential in that regard. We might well look after the few in the 55 to 65 group but we are going to place an unbearable burden on coming generations. We are going to saddle the young married people, the young pioneers whose days of earning are still ahead of them.
The goose can only lay so many golden eggs. This is where I part company with my socialistic friends in the corner, because while the idea of socialism is very attractive I have never heard them offer any answer as to how we are going to pay for it. We hear about shorter hours and bigger wages, but who is going to pay the shot? That is something I should like to know. When you are not in office and do not have the responsibility of paying for things, it is easy to offer bonanzas in one form or another. Although I am not an actuary, I certainly say that what we are really doing is offering a prize packet, but when we open the prize packet it is something like the bacon that we buy these days: The red meat is against the cellophane and all the lard is hidden underneath. In this pension bill we are advertising a false product. We are offering the people of Canada something for nothing, but at the present time the people are in no mood to be fooled by this type of cheap window dressing. They want to know what is under the cellophane in addition to the thin strip of red meat. They want to know how much pale lard is there, and they want to know who is going to have to pay an A grade price for a C grade product.
You will pardon me if I talk in peasant terms. I was raised on a farm and I like to get down to brass tacks. I want to know whether there is bacon in the package or nothing but lard. As I see it, the present pension plan is neither universal nor contributory in a fair way, nor will it be portable once the ambitions of the provincial leaders have full play. I do not think any of the provincial leaders deserve any great kudos at the present time. They all appear to be balkanizing Canada. I should like to see them get together. In fact I think the minister should call them
Canada Pension Plan
together again and tell them to look at the real project, to keep in mind the fair advertising of what we are selling the people of Canada and give them a chance to co-operate and go along with us in a pension plan which is portable, contributory and universal.
I do not like to be merely negative in my criticism. I have what I think is an answer and it is merely coincidental that it happens to agree with certain parts of Mr. Robarts' proposal the other evening. I think our present system of help for the old people of Canada is one of the best in the world from the point of view of being universal and contributory, because if we are able we all pay more or less equally into the plan. It does not have to be portable because at the present time it covers every citizen of Canada who reaches the age of 70. I go along with the idea that this age is somewhat unrealistic. The people who need help most are those who are engaged in the primary industries. It is virtually impossible for them to be effective after the age of 60, and so the age of 65 is approaching a little closer to what I think is a reasonable retirement age for people in this category.
I do not like anything that smells of socialism when it tends to take the fight and initiative out of the individual. I believe in any social justice program which gives security to our senior citizens in their nonproductive years. If this is socialism, then in this narrow sense I go along with it, but I also want to know who is going to pay. There is no such thing as something for nothing in Canada or anywhere else in the world and we can only spend that wealth which we produce. I want to know how this plan is going to be integrated with our plans for producing more wealth and I want to make sure that the people most affected, the hard working family people between the ages of 25 and 55, are going to be able to carry this staggering load.
I sometimes think that the more haste the less speed. We are faced here with the job of unravelling a plan which is going to affect us for perhaps a hundred years. The actuaries who presented briefs to the minister and to parliament quoted figures extending as far as the year 2045. That was the year farthest in the future to which reference was made. So we are tying the hands of future generations well into the middle of the next century. Therefore this is not the time for haste, although the matter is certainly urgent. We have a plan before us already, as I said, as an experiment. It is

Canada Pension Plan
not so many years ago when objections were made that if we made any kind of retirement payment to our old folks it would break the country. At that time the amount was $40. Then it was raised to $46, then $55, then $65 and now the amount is $75. Having in mind the way living costs have mounted, everybody here knows that the present pension of $75 is not worth as much as the $40 pension at the start. We may slap ourselves on the back and say that we are doing very well in improving our pension plan, but we have done no more than try to keep up with the cost of living.
I think this principle is well outlined in the bill. There are clauses in the bill which seek to cover this point but they are not realistic. I understand that no matter what happens within the next two years the old age pensioners could not receive an increase of more than $1.50 per month. The rent can jump much more than that in one month. For example, we heard in the house today that the price of steel is likely to jump $4 a ton. What is this going to do to the cost of living? It may put up the cost of living 3 or 4 per cent but it would still be impossible for these people to get more than $1.50 extra under the present scheme.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be entirely negative, so let me suggest right away that as fast as we can we push legislation through this house to provide for an increase in the old age pension to at least $100 a month, to take effect at age 65 without any means test whatever. I cannot see that any more administration costs would be involved, but we would save considerably by not increasing the civil service payroll or making other wasteful duplications. I think the experiment of paying $75 a month has worked out very well, although it certainly has not satisfied everyone, and I do not suppose that any retirement sum could be set which would satisfy everyone. But if we are to provide for our elderly people a retirement with comfort to meet their needs, then I for one think this figure of $75 is unrealistic. It is no selling point to tell me that 10 years from now, after having paid in to the plan $800, I may be able to increase my own retirement pension by $104 a month. Surely it is a cynical member of this committee who says to me that this is a good scheme, when I refuse to give my own father, who pioneered this country and worked harder than I did in primitive conditions, more than a mere $75 a month while I collect at the same time 
perhaps $179 a month of unpaid for retirement pension.
If we are going to be big shots let us be big shots. If we are going to bear this burden, let us tie it in with a dynamic approach that we will be willing and able to pay for. If we are not willing and able to pay for it I do not think we have the right to saddle it on to our young people. If we cannot show the necessary drive I would be satisfied to take little or nothing of this bonanza of $104 a month, because I would far rather see my father get another $25 a month to provide him with a reasonable bread and butter allowance. Let hon. members stop putting the red strips of bacon under the cellophane in the hope that because they are getting in first or are yelling the loudest they are going to take all the political advantage they can from it, hoping to win a snap election by offering the old people nothing and covering it up with aid to a few in the 55 to 65 age group.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if we are going to have a universal plan, then perhaps this can be thrashed out. I am sure the minister and her government are willing to tailor their cloth somewhat. I would be against anything being compulsory in this plan unless it is universal. I do not think it is right to force self-employed people to pay into a fund which they may not want to pay into, allowing other people to get bonanzas while some may not contribute at all. We are supposed to be a democracy and we should have one law for everyone. If something is to be compulsory I contend that this compulsion automatically should be universal. One Canada, one law. If our provincial leaders have those qualities of leadership which entitle them to be leaders of a state within a state, or a province within the dominion of Canada, I say they should go back to ordinary simple democratic principles and show the leadership to make us one united Canada. Then if they have the ambition and the intention to come to Ottawa and be the big frog in the puddle, then perhaps the people of Canada will be willing to take a second look at them. But if they intend to balkanize Canada they are wasting their time. The people of Canada are looking for the men who are going to make one Canada and who make sure that the same deal is given to each and every one of us.
To me it is ridiculous to add $104 a month to the retirement fund of those who may not need it and some who do not even want it, leaving those people who need it most

at the bottom of the heap. I know it is fun to point to the Conservative party and say that we are the right wing party, the party of the landed gentry. The Conservative party is, and has been for many years, the party of the little people, and it intends to remain the party of the little people. Therefore I hope my appeal is not going to fall on deaf ears, hon. gentlemen opposite describing it as window dressing. It is not window dressing; I am asking for a square deal, something for which we have always worked and for which we intend to go on working.
Some months ago I spoke of certain labour problems in this country, and certain narrow sections of the press called me the enemy of the labouring people because I stood up for the rights of the small labouring man in his own union. What I said on that occasion when I addressed the house was that if we did our duty in the house-and I included myself in that-there would be no need for unions. But I was misunderstood by those who did not hear me, because what I meant to say-
