I say to the committee that in fact we have ranged far away from the principle of the bill, and today more than any other time. It seems to me we have to get

back to examining what it is we are trying to accomplish and to restate the need that must be filled. What is it? It is the fact that 65 per cent, or thereabouts, of employed Canadians are not members of a wage related pension plan, notwithstanding what some have described as the laudable efforts of those who underwrite or offer private pension schemes. It is still an unalterable fact that 65 per cent of Canadians are not members of a wage related pension scheme.
Another significant thing was discovered in the committee hearings, after some 51 meetings, that of those who do retire the greatest mass of beneficiaries under private pension plans find themselves with approximately 40 per cent of their earnings at retirement as their pension benefit. This is an average. There will be many below that figure, and there will be some above it.
It is to fill this need that this bill has been presented to parliament, and the attempts to cry that we are doing nothing for those who are not able to establish a wage related pension are distracting attention from what the bill proposes to do, which is to fill the need I have described.
The bill is also doing something else- settling one major area of controversy-and when you settle one major area of controversy you can then move to improve upon other areas. This is but a first step, and with this area of need filled the government and parliament can then direct their attention prudently, and with more adequate information and enlightenment, to find out what nobody has yet discovered in this chamber- the criteria for an adequate flat rate pension and how far government should go in taxing to provide it.
A lot of members have said that the bill should do more than it does, but there has been a complete dearth of information from those critics as to how the amount of flat rate pension should be calculated. I suggest to the committee that it is impossible to do that job with a sense of responsibility unless you first remove one area of controversy, by filling the need for a wage related pension for those 65 per cent of wage earners who are not now members of a pension plan. This is a deplorable condition and should occupy priority of attention at this time. This is what we are trying to do.
The next question we address ourselves to is, how shall we finance it? In a democracy you propose measures that are politically acceptable and that are generally understood. Our people generally understand that wage

related plans are usually shared 50-50 between the employer and the employee. There is no complexity about that, and so you propose that the contribution to finance it shall be paid 50-50 by the employer and the employee.
If you start to take the funds that are built up for this purpose and produce a lot of universal flat rate benefits, then you are imposing a contribution system which would be truly regressive in the sense that it would be taking more from the low income brackets to make the scheme financially sound. Therefore you must keep the flat rate benefits to an absolute minimum. You do not allow them to go beyond the area of prudence, and I suggest that in this bill flat rate benefits have been prudently and wisely established.
The generally accepted viewpoint among social scientists and economists is that you find the funds for your universal flat rate benefits from a diversity of taxes such as we now have in the income tax field, the sales tax field and the corporation tax field-the so-called 3-3-4 formula. Funds from those sources relieve pressure on people with small incomes; we should rely upon them for social assistance of the kind available under the old age security legislation. Some hon. members have talked a great deal about complexities. Well, there may be difficulty about understanding fully all the excellent and sound projections which have been made by officials of the Department of Finance. The actuarial predictions of our civil servants are certainly complex. But there is nothing complex about the contribution system or about the scale of benefits; a little careful reading will soon acquaint anyone with these provisions. It is true that projections taking into account the impact of this legislation on the economy of Canada in the future do not lend themselves readily to the kind of debate which usually takes place in this house. We must of necessity rely upon the opinions of the authorities. Throughout the 51 meetings we had in the pensions committee there was not one substantial piece of evidence given to us to indicate that our officials had done anything but a sound, capable and well informed job. They had made projections which give us a real picture of the economic implications of this plan. There is no question about that.
Those who oppose the plan have not seen fit to discuss it in terms of actuarial accuracy or economic soundness. They have been directing their attention to the old age security field, entirely away from the purpose

of this bill. It seems to me we should pause before making a lot of suggestions about other areas of activity. I believe we should resolve this controversy about a wage related plan first. There are many small employers who cannot afford the cost of an underwritten plan such as is now privately available to them; they are just waiting for this question to be settled so that they can go ahead and work out a private plan to supplement the Canada pension plan through their own efforts. In this way they would be contributing by their savings to the strength of the economy.
I suggest that no one has yet placed before this house a comprehensive, well reasoned and well documented statement as to the impact on the economy involved in a proposal to increase offhand the amounts which are proposed in this measure. There has been no statement based in any way on actuarial calculations, and until such submissions have been made we can only conclude that those suggestions are irresponsible and ill-founded -that they are in fact nothing more than a tactical political move for the sake of political advantage.

At that time I took some care to do some research as to the purchasing value of the dollar. According to a table which was presented to me by some well informed individuals, based on the purchasing power of the dollar in 1939 as being 100 per cent, the purchasing power of the dollar in 1820 was two dollars and fourteen point six cents. In 1964, in relation to this table, the purchasing power of the dollar was approximately 50 cents. In the light of those facts it is very fortunate, indeed, that this bill provides for an adjustment in pensions payable in relation to the purchasing power of the dollar.

that they are excluded as beneficiaries under this bill, and I refer to the 1,500,000 senior employees whose age and income prohibits them from receiving the benefits of a pension plan based on the provisions of this bill.

Penalizes low incomes.

When I am finished. You may have even more questions to ask me then. I raise this point specifically at this time because the question is a pertinent one. Are these people with old age security of $75 a month, which is all they are going to get, in a position to enjoy security with dignity?
I want to put on record, because it is pertinent to this problem, one paragraph from

Canada Pension Plan
the second volume of the Hall commission report. We are told that the plan covers all Canadians, and somehow or other through Bill No. C-136 we are going to give them security with dignity. At page 265 of the second volume of the royal commission on health services report it is stated:
In discussing in volume I the particular health problems of the north, we have referred to the inhuman living conditions we found in some settlements. Those conditions are not common to all parts of the territories but they are sufficiently widespread-
And these are pertinent words.
-to cause alarm and demand quick and determined action. The contrast between the primitive conditions of those vegetating in tents and snow-houses with those of officials living in houses providing most of the comforts we know in the south, only serves to accentuate the plight of the former group. We must assume that Canadians have been only dimly aware of these circumstances, which would not be tolerated anywhere else. Even in the more bearable climate of the south, no one would be allowed to even spend one night, let alone a whole winter, or a lifetime under such degrading conditions.
This is a situation which Bill No. C-136 is designed to correct, if I can accept the hon. lady's statement that it is to establish as soon as possible a fair and practical way in which all Canadians will be able to retire in security and with dignity. But the vast majority of these poor people are going to get nothing out of the Canada pension plan as now proposed. I realize we are going to be in the middle of an election campaign one of these fine months, and I can well imagine the kind of things which are going to be said, and this divinely inspired statement in the white paper giving all Canadians security with dignity is going to be one of the statements used.
I suggest to the hon. lady that if she and her government are going to do nothing to give assistance to these people in any national plan, I have another campaign slogan which she had better use, and it is this: "Nothing is too good for the people of the north". Because that is what the Liberals are giving them-nothing.

I want from the government benches an explanation of whether or not the Canadian Indians and Eskimo are considered full Canadians within the ambit of the description "all Canadians". If they are, why
is it that they are going to get nothing out of this plan? Do they have a right to expect this?
What have they been promised, Mr. Chairman? I have told the committee what the hon. lady promised them, but what about the Prime Minister? He visited this same group of Eskimo people and made promises to them. I do not know whether he remembers his promises; after all, he has a certain kind of selective amnesia which is extremely fascinating; but if he remembers, he promised these people that under his guidance there would be no difference between them and other Canadians. He said, smiling benignly upon them, "There is no difference between us, we are all the same". I want to know whether these Canadians are going to be given any assistance under this Bill No. C-136.
What about the people, Mr. Chairman, who are already old? Let us see how the philosophy which is enunciated in this white paper stands up. Are the old people who are now retired classified as Canadians? The criterion applied is a bare $75 a month for those who are aged today. Is this a practical way to meet the needs of our elderly people? Is $75 a month going to provide dignity and security? How many hundreds of thousands of southern Canadians are in this category? What about those who are disabled; are they Canadians? What about those who are widowed or orphaned? Do these people have the right to dignity and security? What about all those who will become widowed in the next three years, or will become disabled within the next five years, or who will lose their parents and will become orphans? Are these people Canadians? Do they have the right to dignity and security? Because under the Canada pension plan they are going to get absolutely nothing now and nothing in the future. Indeed, estimates have been made that as many as 2.5 million Canadians are not going to be covered by this plan. I know the hon. lady as recently as 20 months ago was addicted to the truth, but what I should like her to do now is to give this committee an honest statement as to what Bill No. C-136 will in fact accomplish; and this is what we will vote on in this committee.
The statement in the white paper is not an accurate statement. I am going to read, Mr. Chairman, what in fact will be an accurate statement of what the plan will do, amending the statement made in the white paper as best I can. First of all, let me read the original

Canada Pension Plan
statement again, because it is a priceless piece of creative writing:
This is to establish a contributory pension plan ensuring that, as soon as is possible in a fair and practical way, all Canadians will be able to look forward to retiring in security and with dignity.
This is how the statement, as amended, would have to read:
This is to establish a contributory pension plan ensuring that...some Canadians will be able to .. .retire.
And that is about all the plan does, if you strip that sentence of its adjectives and of the words which will appear on the next federal election campaign posters. That is in fact a truthful statement of what Bill No. C-136 does.
Other things are said in the white paper with which I do not intend to bother the committee. It promises that the plan will be nation-wide in character. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if 80 per cent of the residents of the Yukon and Northwest Territories are not even eligible for the plan, how is it going to be nation-wide? Indeed, the only element of portability that I will not question at all is in the case of the two and a half million Canadians who are going to get nothing, because it is not very difficult to carry nothing from one part of the country to another.
May I say I have some serious questions about the funds which will be made available to the provinces, and here I am speaking primarily as a northerner. Because as I understand it, the funds which will be made available to the provincial authorities will depend on the contributions raised in a given area. So where does this principle leave the have-not areas of the country, such as Canada's northern region, the Yukon and Northwest Territories? Surely if there is one area in need of an imaginative development program it is that area. Are we merely going to return all those dollars that will be collected under the Canada pension plan from the handful of people who will be eligible to join it in the far north?
What about some of the administrative problems? I am not going to labour the fact that there will be a new army of federal officials. It is the Department of Labour which will be numbering everyone. It is the Department of National Revenue which will collect, and the Department of National Health and Welfare which will give out. Anyone with experience of such programs knows that when one federal department attempts to administer them it runs into serious problems. My God, what will be the situation

with three different departments in the act, all drawing up files? Every year we have a new child in our family they will want to issue a new number and the flies will mount up.
In the committee hearings we discussed the problems of calculating the pensions according to formulae very few people can understand, including the expert witnesses who appeared before the committee. The formula involved is one that would give Einstein a headache, but we were assured they were going to buy computers to do this, that they could put a card in one end and out of the other end would come the figure of, say, $54.17 to be paid to a widow living in Winnipeg. Then if they want to verify this fact they will merely run another card in another computer which will give the same figure.
Is the government going to provide a computer to each member of parliament to handle the sacks of mail that will arrive from people living in the same community, in apparently identical circumstances, and who receive different pensions? What about the 1,200,000 applications a year for refunds which, according to the experts advising the committee, can be expected to be received from people who overpay to the Canada pension plan? What computer is going to handle that?
I am happy to see the new and amiable Minister of National Revenue in his chair, because we are discussing administrative problems, particularly as they apply to my neck of the woods. I invite the Minister of National Health and Welfare to ask him about the problems of trying to administer income tax matters in the Canadian north, and to read the answer he gave me two days ago saying they have not been able to establish a district taxation office in the Canadian north. If they cannot do that, how in the world are they going to administer a plan for people scattered over 1,600,000 square miles of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon?

I would hope that somehow or other the hon. lady would see fit to amend this plan. All I want her to do is make it conform to her word. This is a very simple definition of truth. It is whether or not your plan conforms to what you are saying, whether or not your thoughts and your words conform. I invite her to use that kind of

yardstick in the next election campaign in terms of what is truth.
I want the plan to include all Canadians and I would do anything in my power to assist and support a plan that would do that. We have had suggestions made as to how it could be done. We have asked that all people be eligible to receive benefits under the Canada pension plan. We have asked that the old age security be increased to $100 a month to cover all those in circumstances where they will get nothing from the pension plan.
I am alarmed and concerned when I listen to a speech such as that made tonight by the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) who said, "Don't worry, this plan does not cover all Canadians. It does not meet all needs. We are not trying to do that, but if you will do this for us you will get rid of this one area and we will then be free to go on and plan in a common sense prudent manner to meet the needs of the other people". When the hon. member for Kootenay West tried to get a specific commitment from the minister that this in fact was what the government was planning, why in the world could the ministry not take us into its confidence?
I am extremely concerned when a federal government collects upwards of $600 million a year and admits it is not meeting the most pressing problems of the day, saying, "Let's do this first and then we will talk about the aged and the disabled." This chamber has to ask itself, should the state set up a vast bureaucracy, a vast mechanism of tax collection and take in $600 million a year of taxation-this is what it is-at a time when it is not prepared to redistribute it to the areas of most need, and is not even prepared to give us a commitment on what its plans are to meet other needs.
Reviewing the history of the government gives a thinking person even more cause to be concerned, because I have a hunch that the Canadian people are going to be told, indeed that they already believe, that all their needs will be met in some mysterious way by this complicated piece of legislation. I have a hunch that it will not be until after the next election that they will find out that if they are now old, disabled, widowed or orphaned, or become so in the next three or five years, they will get absolutely nothing.
In other words, I am afraid that by adopting this program we will postpone the day when the federal government will sit down with the provincial governments, as requested
Canada Pension Plan
by some of the provincial premiers, to look at those areas of unmet pressing social needs. I am afraid people will be told, "Don't worry, you have got the Canada pension plan," and the bitter truth is that they are going to get absolutely nothing out of it, a truth which will not become apparent until after the next election.
I urge the minister to get up in the committee at any time and admit that people who are now old and retired will get absolutely nothing out of the Canada pension plan. She is a great advocate of truth. Why will she not say that, because that in fact is the truth under this present bill? I want her to get up and say, "Anyone who is now a widow will get absolutely nothing from the Canada pension plan." I want her to say, "All of you who are now disabled are going to get nothing out of the Canada pension plan." I want her to go to the voters in the next election, not with this piece of imaginative fiction about all Canadians retiring in security and with dignity, but to say that there will be nothing for orphans in the next five years, nothing for the disabled in the next five years, and nothing for widows in the next five years.
I have a final plea to make. I for one would be prepared to put up with a slight delay in the implementation of the plan if there were any hope whatever that it could in fact become a national pension plan including all the provinces. It seems to me there is not very much separating the present proposal from such a proposal which would be acceptable to all provinces. I should like the Prime Minister to give some leadership in this regard-to sit down and take a look at it, along with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and his $25,000 a year coordinator, in the light of all that the committee has discussed. I am sure there is a possibility that all the provinces would agree and we could in fact have a truly national pension plan. If this could be achieved I submit it would be worth the extra time it might take. The day the minister indicates in some manner that she is prepared to include all Canadians in the plan is the day I shall be able to vote for her plan wholeheartedlj' knowing that it will ensure-these words are so beautiful I have to read them again-"that as soon as possible in a fair and practical way all Canadians will be able to look forward to retiring with security and with dignity."

I hasten to answer the questions posed by the hon. member. We did

Canada Pension Plan
indeed spend a few hours with some of his constituents on Baffin island. There I had an opportunity to see the way in which the Eskimos of Frobisher Bay, at least, lived. I learned that many of them are employed by the federal government, though many of them are not employed and often have little cash income.	.
What the hon. member said to the native people of the northern region of Canada then is not of a piece with what he has said this evening, segregating them from all other Canadians. He tried to say this evening that there is something different about Eskimos and Indians which sets them apart from other Canadians. I am astonished he should do so as their representative because it is clear that Indians and Eskimos are treated under the Canada pension plan in exactly the same way as all other Canadians. Those who do not work are not included whether they be Indians, Eskimos or anyone else.

That is correct. I was referring to those who are not in the labour force, those who do not have wage income. Those who do have income will receive, subsequently, a proportionate pension because they will have made proportionate payment of their income. The hon. member suggests the vast majority will get nothing from this proposal. I demur; it is not correct. The vast majority will get at least 150 per cent of their present income, for if they now have an income of $600 or less they will, by virtue of the Prime Minister's announcement, receive as a minimum $900 a year when they reach the age of 65. In other words they will be in the same position as any other Canadian in similar circumstances.
I might also say that the hon. member has tried to indicate he was led to believe that every last Canadian, every last baby in its cradle, would be covered by the Canada pension plan. We all know he is too intelligent to pass that off in this chamber. From the beginning every hon. member has known that this was to be a wage related plan linked with people who are in employment and who earn wages. The hon. member has therefore sought by sophistry to infer that there has been some change or some attempt to mislead the house at some time in the past. I have

some figures here in which he may be interested. According to the estimates of the labour force, in 1964 there were 6,920,000 persons in the Canadian labour force. The estimates which have been prepared indicate that the Canada pension plan will cover 6,373,000 of them or more than 92 per cent of the Canadian work force.

Mr. Chairman, the previous speaker mentioned a moment ago that we should change the wording of the white paper as it is a plan enabling the smallest number of Canadians to retire with dignity and in security.
I wonder if a few sentences could not be replaced in order to say that the purpose of this plan is to remedy the weaknesses of the Canadian taxation program and make up for the administrative deficits of the various governments. I think the purpose of this plan is not to achieve the great social security to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) referred when she spoke about a contributory pension plan for the benefit of the greatest number of Canadians.
After this bill was considered by a committee, sent back to the house and discussed by the official opposition, we all realized, with a few exceptions, that the number of people who would be excluded or would not benefit from this proposed contributory pension plan would be such that it would be readily seen that a very large number of Canadians would get no benefit at all and would not retire with dignity and in security.
Second, if you consider these words, "retired in security and dignity", you find that a great number of Canadians not living at present in security and dignity will nevertheless be subjected to contributions, since those having an income of $600 will be included in this vast group of contributors to

a social security plan allowing retirement in security and dignity.
Those are high sounding words and sentences, words which, as was mentioned by the member who spoke before me, will surely strike the imagination of voters at the next election: federal pension plan advocated by the Liberal party, the party of great men and great achievements, and which will make it possible for workers to retire in security and dignity even though more than two million Canadians do not even earn a taxable income, that is more than $2,000 a year. Those people surely live in the worst state of indignity and insecurity in Canada and yet it is precisely that huge group of workers which will have to pay contributions to build up a pension fund out of which they will get $50 or $100 and some odd dollars when they reach the retirement age.
The proposed scheme has many weaknesses. It has been recognized that the plan cannot truly be considered as a social security program, as several hon. members call it, because a social security plan which further deprives those who already earn too little to cope with the cost of living while they are working, does not allow the latter to live in dignity and security.
This project should certainly not be considered as a comprehensive social security plan. As others have already pointed out, it will surely result in an increased cost of living. This was mentioned in committee, and I noted that in the house other members referred earlier to a possible increase in the cost of living.
I admit that the proposed plan takes into account this increase which will necessarily result from the employers' contributions, because they will certainly have a great deal of work to do in order to establish standards as complicated as those required by such a pension plan.
No contributor will be able to check his benefits, because he will not have access to these automatic computers. We have heard about computers. These contributors will have to be satisfied with the information passed on to them by the plan administrators, and worse than that, they will have to take on the interest burden as well, when the administrators have invested these funds at any level of government. Thus, provincial governments which have secured from the pension fund certain loans for some works within their own field, such as roads or school construction, even at a minimum interest, will have to repay, in 20 years, out of the taxpayers' 20220-738
Canada Pension Plan
money the amounts loaned to them and bear the tax burden in 1980, 1990, to pay a second time, part of the pension the contributors will receive when they reach 65 years of age.
Can we boast that we are establishing in this country a social security program in which all Canadians will be proud to take part? I do not think so.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that Quebec is not directly participating in the pension plan that the other nine provinces seem to be accepting now, although under this co-operative federalism for which the foundations have been laid, enough meetings have been held to lead the people to believe that the Quebec pension plan will meet exactly the standards of the federal plan now before us. But I wonder whether it was not rather the federal plan that was adapted to the standards of the contributory pension plan of the Quebec government, which was studied before and during the federal-provincial conference of March 25, 1964.
I remember that, at that time, some friends in the Liberal party told me: "We are rather proud, we, federal members of parliament from Quebec, that Quebec does not accept the federal plan as a whole, because the provincial government will have the hateful job of collecting the contributions. That means that already some federal Liberal members recognized the hatefulness of collecting contributions from small wage earners, those whose yearly income of $2,000 or $3,000 is already inadequate to enable them to give their dependants a decent and dignified livelihood.
Consequently, if it was recognized that the hateful aspect of collecting the contributions would fall on the Quebec government and if some federal Liberal members of parliament even rejoiced, I wonder how it is possible to approve with such enthusiasm a pension plan identical to that which the Quebec legislature intends to approve shortly?
As I pointed out earlier, this will not solve the problem either. In 20 years from now, the same taxpayers who will have contributed to enable the provincial government to set up or administer a contributory pension plan, will have to pay once again the amounts to be repaid eventually.
Provincial governments will invest money in non-economic undertakings, such as bridge and road building and building of similar things that are certainly not as productive as those in which private enterprises invest money to increase their production capacity. Therefore one must admit in advance that by

Canada Pension Plan
1980-90, the cost of this so-called social security that is said to be the finest of all the measures voted by the Canadian government on behalf of their fellow-citizens will already be twice as great.
Mr. Chairman, it was even suggested a while ago that there had not been throughout the 51 meetings of this committee, any specialist or expert to provide something of a really constructive nature. However, a good number of them said rather clearly, I believe, that the 1.8 per cent contribution from the worker and the 1.8 per cent from the employer, which are now being proposed, were merely used as a basic principle. In fact, the actuaries of various companies, namely those who drafted the U.S. social
security plan, appeared before the said committee and said that, 20 years from now, in all likelihood, the plan would require a 4 per cent contribution from the employee as well as the employer. They are misleading the population; they promote the idea of a large social security plan but fail to say exactly how much it will cost all Canadians to get only some of them to benefit from that old age pension plan.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock? [Text]
Progress reported.
